units.title: Section 1: Rights, the law and the legal system in England and Wales

outcomes.text: Explain and analyse the human, moral, legal and political rights, duties, equalities and freedoms that citizens hold.
State the age of criminal responsibility and other legal ages at which young people become responsible, such as driving, marrying, voting or joining the armed forces.
Explain and evaluate the justifications for these age laws.

subtopics.title: Magna Carta and human rights law

outcomes.text: Describe the background to Magna Carta and its main provisions, and explain its significance for the development of rights.
Outline the main provisions of the UDHR, the European Convention on Human Rights, the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Human Rights Act 1998, and why they protect rights.
Use this knowledge to evaluate how governments around the world act on rights.
Explain the right to representation, including the role and history of trade unions and employee associations.
Evaluate how effectively different organisations support and represent their members.
Analyse rights in local, national and global situations where they conflict.
Evaluate outcomes where rights and responsibilities must be balanced, using local, national and global examples.
Describe the nature of rules and laws.
Explain how rules and laws help society deal with problems of fairness, justice and discrimination.
Explain the fundamental principles of law that protect rights and freedoms, keep order and resolve conflicts, and apply them to examples.
Explain the presumption of innocence and equality before the law.
Evaluate the effectiveness of at least one piece of legislation.
Distinguish criminal law from civil law and apply this to specific examples.
Identify the main sources of law (common law, legislation, judge-made precedent) and apply them to examples.
Identify the different legal jurisdictions of the UK: Northern Ireland, Scotland, England and Wales.
Explain how the justice system operates: police roles and powers, the judiciary, legal representatives, criminal and civil courts, tribunals and other dispute resolution.
Explain how the youth justice system operates.
Describe the roles and responsibilities of citizens as jurors, magistrates, special constables, police commissioners and tribunal members.
Evaluate how effective these citizen roles are in the legal system.
Explain the factors that affect crime rates in society and evaluate strategies to reduce crime.
Explain the nature and purpose of different sanctions for criminal offences.
Evaluate the effects of different sanctions on offenders and their families, victims and their families, and wider society.

topics.title: 2.1 Democracy, elections and voting in the UK

outcomes.text: Explain the concept of democracy and the key features of democratic government: free regular elections, secret ballots, an inclusive franchise and a choice of candidates or parties.
Distinguish classical democracy from representative democracy.
Explain that the UK is a representative democracy with a sovereign parliament and MPs who represent constituencies.

subtopics.title: Voting and holding power to account

outcomes.text: State who can and cannot vote in UK parliamentary elections.
Identify the ways citizens can contribute to parliamentary democracy and hold those in power to account.
Explain the rights and responsibilities that apply in a representative democracy.
Explain why the rule of law, personal freedom, tolerance and respect for diversity, and equal opportunity matter for effective democratic government.
Name the major UK political parties.
Explain the main philosophical and political differences between the parties.
Describe the electoral systems used in the UK: first-past-the-post, Additional Member System, Single Transferable Vote, and referendums.
Explain how electoral systems affect election outcomes and the composition of governments.
Weigh the advantages and disadvantages of these systems.

topics.title: 2.2 National, local, regional and devolved government

outcomes.text: Explain how large parties can govern alone or in coalition.
Explain how governments are formed after a parliamentary or assembly election.
Describe the key roles of the Prime Minister, Cabinet and ministers.
Describe the role, structure and organisation of local, regional and devolved government in the UK.
Explain the changing relationships between England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.
Explain the reasons for devolution and centralisation, and evaluate arguments for further devolution.
Distinguish the separate but complementary roles of the executive, legislature, judiciary and Monarchy.
Explain how Parliament holds government to account through oversight and scrutiny, and that Parliament is sovereign.
Explain why these roles are kept separate.
Describe the roles of the House of Commons, House of Lords and Monarch in a bicameral parliament and how they differ.
Weigh the advantages and disadvantages of a bicameral arrangement.
Describe the roles of front and back bench MPs, the Commons Speaker and party whips.
Describe key ceremonial occasions: State Opening of Parliament, the budget, the Monarch's speech and Black Rod.
Explain how parliamentary candidates are selected and the role of citizens in this.
Explain how parliamentary debate and decision-making shape policy and legislation.
Explain the role and importance of the official Opposition.
Explain that government administration is split into departments, ministries and agencies.
Explain the role of the civil service and the police within the British constitution.
Explain how institutional relationships form an uncodified constitution.
Explain why tensions arise between institutions and how their relationships are changing.
Describe how local and national government raise public taxes.
Identify the main areas of public expenditure for local and national government.
Explain the relationships between taxation, administrative efficiency, economic growth and public spending.

subtopics.title: Spending decisions and value for money

outcomes.text: Explain how governments weigh these relationships and political factors to manage risk and make spending decisions that give value for money.
Analyse and evaluate different viewpoints on taxation.
Analyse and evaluate debates about government provision for welfare, health, education and the needs of the elderly.

topics.title: 2.5 The role of the media and free press

outcomes.text: Describe the legal rights and responsibilities of a free press.
Explain the media's moral responsibility to report accurately and respect privacy and dignity.
Explain the media's roles in informing and influencing opinion, providing a forum for ideas and holding the powerful to account.
Evaluate how effectively the media carries out these roles.
Describe how media regulation works in the UK.
Explain the reasons for media regulation and censorship.
Evaluate the effectiveness of media regulation.
Analyse how groups wishing to influence public opinion use the media.
Analyse how those in power use the media.
Describe the role of citizens in the UK constitution.
Describe the opportunities for citizen participation in UK democracy, including the National Citizen Service.
Identify barriers to participation and explain why participation matters for a democracy.
Explain the potential impact of social media and digital democracy on participation and voter engagement.
Analyse and evaluate measures designed to increase participation and voter engagement.

Describe the actions citizens can take to promote viewpoints and hold power to account: interest groups, trade unions, parties, standing for election, campaigning, lobbying, petitions and demonstrations.
Explain the importance of accountability in a representative democracy.
Analyse the roles of public institutions, services, pressure groups, unions, charities and voluntary groups in giving citizens a voice and support.
Analyse and evaluate two examples of citizens changing or improving their communities.
Take part in a planned course of informed Citizenship Action.
Describe ways citizens contribute to wider public life, including interest groups, advocacy and volunteering, and why this matters in a democracy.
Compare the nature and extent of citizens' political participation in the UK with one other democratic system.
Compare citizens' political participation in the UK with one non-democratic system.
Evaluate how far the UK embodies democratic values compared with other governments.

units.title: Section 3: The UK and the wider world

topics.title: 3.1 Identities and diversity in UK society

outcomes.text: Identify the main factors affecting people's sense of identity at individual, group, national and global scales.
Name the UK's constituent nations and explain how connections to them shape identity.
Explain why people hold multiple, complex identities in UK society.
Explain why people migrate from one place to another.
Describe the broad patterns of migration into and out of the UK over the last 60 years and the reasons behind them.
Explain what seeking asylum means and why people seek it.
Analyse the main benefits of immigration to the UK and its impact on communities.
Analyse the main challenges of immigration and its impact on communities.
Evaluate different viewpoints on controlling immigration.
Explain why mutual respect, understanding and community cohesion matter in a democratic society.
Analyse the factors that promote community cohesion, including democratic values.
Analyse and evaluate citizen actions that have sought to improve community cohesion.

topics.title: 3.2 The UK and its relations with the wider world

outcomes.text: Name the international organisations the UK belongs to (UN and agencies, NATO, Council of Europe, Commonwealth, WTO) and outline their other members.
State the aims of these organisations, why they were set up, why the UK belongs and what role it plays.
Evaluate how far the United Nations has met its aims.

subtopics.title: The UK and the European Union

outcomes.text: Describe the principles behind the formation and development of the European Union.
Analyse the benefits and costs of the UK leaving the EU.
Analyse the impact on the UK of one EU decision.
Evaluate the quality and effectiveness of the current UK-EU relationship.
Describe the methods governments can use to intervene in international disputes or crises: practical support, mediation, sanctions or force.
Analyse and evaluate the UK government's role and contribution in one international crisis, dispute or conflict.
Explain why international agreements are needed to protect victims of conflict and set rules of warfare.
Analyse the provisions of International Humanitarian Law.
Evaluate how far it has protected civilians in one modern conflict.
Analyse the role of one international NGO in a crisis and evaluate the effects of its intervention.
Explain why international NGOs may be more effective than governments in these roles.

As a team, research and evaluate a citizenship issue using primary and secondary sources, linking it to rights and responsibilities, participation and media, the law, and British values and diversity.
Describe and explain your own viewpoint and others' viewpoints using the evidence gathered.
Plan an appropriate Citizenship Action in collaboration with others, using primary and secondary research.
Carry out a Citizenship Action with others that involves problem-solving and advocacy.
Critically evaluate the action as a whole, including what went well and what to improve.
Explain how actions affect local, national and global settings and how an action could be enlarged.
